title: Anderson v. Intel Corporation Investment Policy Committee
backgroundAndFacts:
Winston R. Anderson and other current and former Intel employees participated in Intel's 401(k) retirement plan, which is governed by a federal law called ERISA (the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974). They sued Intel's Investment Policy Committee, the group responsible for managing the plan's investments, alleging that the committee violated its fiduciary duty by offering poorly performing and excessively expensive investment options—including certain hedge funds and private equity funds—that cost plan participants millions of dollars in retirement savings.

The federal district court dismissed the lawsuit at an early stage, ruling that the plaintiffs had not adequately pleaded their claims. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the dismissal, holding that ERISA plaintiffs must not only allege that fiduciaries breached their duties but must also plausibly allege that the breach actually caused a loss to the plan. Because the plaintiffs had not sufficiently connected Intel's investment choices to concrete financial harm, the appeals court said the case could not proceed.

The plaintiffs petitioned the Supreme Court, arguing that the Ninth Circuit's requirement improperly shifts the burden onto employees who are suing to protect their retirement savings. They contend that under ERISA, once a plaintiff shows a fiduciary breach, the burden falls on the fiduciary—not the employee—to prove that the breach did not cause any loss. The case raises fundamental questions about how hard it is for retirement plan participants to get their day in court when they believe their plan managers have mishandled their money.
legalQuestion: Whether ERISA plaintiffs must plausibly allege in their complaint that a fiduciary breach actually caused financial losses to the plan, or whether causation is an affirmative defense that fiduciaries must raise and prove.
significance:
This case could significantly affect the retirement security of millions of American workers who participate in employer-sponsored 401(k) and pension plans. If the Supreme Court sides with the employees, it will be easier for plan participants to bring ERISA breach-of-fiduciary-duty lawsuits past the initial pleading stage, potentially holding plan managers more accountable for poor investment decisions. If the Court sides with Intel, plan administrators and employers will have a powerful early defense that could shield them from litigation even when investment choices appear imprudent.

The decision will also resolve a legal question about who bears the burden of proving—or disproving—causation in ERISA fiduciary breach cases. Courts of appeals have approached this question inconsistently, and a Supreme Court ruling will establish a uniform national standard. Given that ERISA governs retirement plans covering tens of millions of workers, the outcome will shape how plan fiduciaries make investment decisions and how aggressively they can be held accountable for those choices.

parties.coreArgument: ERISA's statutory text and structure place the burden of proving that a fiduciary breach did not cause a loss on the fiduciary, not on the plan participants who bring suit. Requiring employees to plead and prove causation at the complaint stage misreads ERISA and makes it nearly impossible for retirement savers to vindicate their rights.
supportingPoints: ERISA Section 409 imposes liability on fiduciaries for losses resulting from a breach, and the Act's burden-shifting framework puts the burden on the breaching fiduciary to show the loss was not caused by the breach.
Demanding causation at the pleading stage is especially unfair because employees lack access to the plan's internal investment data and decision-making records before discovery.

The Ninth Circuit's heightened pleading standard conflicts with how other circuits handle ERISA fiduciary duty claims, creating an uneven playing field for retirement savers depending on where they live.

Intel's selection of high-cost, underperforming alternative investments like hedge funds and private equity funds was itself sufficient evidence of a plausible breach that should survive a motion to dismiss.

parties.party: Intel Corporation Investment Policy Committee, et al. (Respondents)
parties.coreArgument: ERISA plaintiffs must plausibly allege that a fiduciary breach actually caused harm to the plan in order to state a viable claim, because loss causation is an element of the claim, not an affirmative defense. Allowing meritless ERISA suits to proceed past the pleading stage imposes enormous costs on plan sponsors and ultimately harms the very participants the law is designed to protect.
supportingPoints: ERISA Section 409's requirement that losses result 'from' a breach naturally imposes causation as part of the plaintiff's burden, consistent with ordinary tort principles.
The Supreme Court's pleading standards under Twombly and Iqbal require plaintiffs to allege factual matter that plausibly supports all elements of their claim, including causation.

Allowing ERISA suits to proceed without a plausible causation allegation would expose plan fiduciaries to costly discovery and settlement pressure even when investment decisions were prudent and well-reasoned.

Sophisticated investment options like hedge funds and private equity are legitimate, diversifying choices for large retirement plans, and courts should not second-guess prudent fiduciary decisions without a concrete showing of harm.

citedPrecedents.reasonCited: Affirmed that ERISA fiduciaries have an ongoing duty to monitor plan investments and remove imprudent ones, which underpins petitioners' argument that Intel's continued offering of poor investment options was a sustained breach.

Established the federal pleading standard requiring complaints to contain sufficient factual matter to state a plausible claim for relief, which respondents argue requires petitioners to plead causation.

Extended Twombly's plausibility pleading standard to all civil cases, and respondents rely on it to argue that ERISA plaintiffs must plausibly plead every element of their claim, including that the breach caused a loss.
Addressed the pleading standard for ERISA fiduciary duty claims involving company stock funds, and petitioners argue its reasoning supports a more permissive approach to ERISA pleading generally.

Interpreted ERISA's remedial provisions broadly and distinguished between the elements of a claim and affirmative defenses, relevant to the question of which party bears the burden of proving causation.

citedPrecedents.caseName: LaRue v. DeWolff, Boberg & Associates, Inc.
citedPrecedents.reasonCited: Confirmed that individual plan participants can bring ERISA fiduciary breach claims to recover losses to their individual accounts in defined contribution plans like 401(k)s, establishing the right to sue that petitioners exercise here.
